verdict.reasoning: Patient reports 5-day history of cough and constant nasal discharge: "five days ago I started having problems like a cough and my nose is just constantly streaming."
Patient describes dry cough every 20–30 minutes: "It's quite bad. It's kind of quite dry. I'm coughing maybe every 20, 30 minutes or so."
Patient denies sputum production: Doctor: "Are you bringing up any phlegm at all?" Patient: "No, no."
Patient denies hemoptysis: Doctor: "Have you coughed up any blood or anything like that?" Patient: "Nope."
Patient reports green nasal discharge: Doctor: "And any blood coming from the nose?" Patient: "No, it's pretty green."
Patient describes feeling hot with chills: "I've been feeling really hot... like to touch. I'm quite hot, but sometimes I'm feeling really chilly, needing to be under a blanket."
Patient reports muscle aches: "No, I've had quite achy muscles, but that's pretty much it."
Patient had transient diarrhea at onset that resolved: "around when it started. I had some diarrhea... But since then it's all been pretty fine." and later denies current diarrhea.
Recent blood test ~3 weeks ago was normal: Doctor: "with your diabetes, have you had a blood test recently?" Patient: "Yeah, like. Yeah, it was normal. It was around three weeks ago."

Patient has not checked temperature and is advised to buy a thermometer: "Have you checked your temperature with a thermometer?" Patient: "No, I haven't." and later Doctor: "it's definitely worth getting a thermometer..."
Patient lacks glucose meter at current location: Doctor: "Do you have blood sugar checking equipment?" Patient: "I'm not at home, no." This supports no home glucose checks today.
Diabetes mellitus is documented: Patient: "I'm diabetic" and later confirms diabetes as a medical problem.
Hypertension is documented: Patient: "I've got hypertension, so I'm on some drugs for that." and "Just the hypertension and the diabetes."
Transcript confirms diabetes and a normal blood test 3 weeks ago but never specifies type 2 or explicitly that diabetes is "stable": only "Yeah, like. Yeah, it was normal."

Hypertension treated with lisinopril and recent BP unknown: Patient lists lisinopril as a drug; Doctor asks "when did you last have your blood pressure checked?" Patient: "A while ago." and "Do you know if it's unstable?" Patient: "I can't remember."
Metformin use documented: Patient: "I think something called metformin and lisinopril, I think, is the other one."
Lisinopril and dose "200" documented: Patient: "metformin and lisinopril" and later Doctor: "do you know what dose of the lisinopril you're taking?" Patient: "200."

Lemsip use 2–3 times/day documented: Patient: "Quite a few Lem Zips..." Doctor: "How many in a day do you normally take?" Patient: "Maybe two or three. Maybe, like, at the start of the day and at the end of the day."

Doctor states Lemsip contains paracetamol: "What you're doing at the moment with the lemcip I wouldn't take. And that contains paracetamol, so don't take any other paracetamol containing products with that."
There is no explicit instruction to continue metformin; continuation can be inferred but is not stated as a specific plan.
There is no explicit instruction to continue lisinopril; this is not directly stated in the plan.
Seasonal hay fever reported: Doctor: "Do you have any allergies to anything?" Patient: "I sometimes suffer from some, like hay fever."
Living situation documented: Doctor: "Who do you live with at home?" Patient: "My partner and my dog."
Occupation documented: Doctor: "And do you work?" Patient: "Yes, I'm an office manager."
Non-smoker status documented: Doctor: "And do you smoke at all?" Patient: "No."
Occasional sherry documented: Doctor: "Do you drink any alcohol?" Patient: "Yes, the odd sherry."

Doctor assesses likely chest infection, likely viral, with nasal and chest symptoms and fever: "it sounds like you... probably have got an infection in the chest... most of the time. These infections are caused by viruses" plus 5 days of dry cough and green nasal discharge and febrile symptoms are documented earlier.
While diabetes and normal blood tests are noted and no home glucose checks today is supported, the note never specifies "type 2" or explicitly calls the diabetes "stable."
Hypertension on lisinopril with BP status unknown is supported: lisinopril listed; last BP check was "a while ago" and patient "can't remember" if it's unstable.
Current Lemsip use and paracetamol content are stated, and doctor warns about duplicate paracetamol: "that contains paracetamol, so don't take any other paracetamol containing products with that."

Doctor expects viral self-resolution over 1–2 weeks and advises symptomatic care: "most of the time. These infections are caused by viruses, so they do normally settle by themselves, but it can take, you know, a week or two" and recommends continuing current symptomatic measures.

Doctor advises getting a thermometer from a pharmacy: "it's definitely worth getting a thermometer and checking your temperature." Patient: "I can just get one of those at a pharmacy or something." Doctor agrees.

Red-flag thresholds are given: "if the temperature is ongoing above 37.5, 38... or your cough's getting worse, you're coughing up lots of nasty phlegm or you cough up any blood or get blood coming out your nose or any shortness of breath, chest pain, then we certainly would need to speak to you again."

Antibiotics only if worsening/persistent fever or deterioration, especially with diabetes: Doctor discusses likely viral cause and then: "If it's not settling or the temperatures ongoing getting worse, then we definitely need to talk to you again." and mentions diabetes increases bacterial infection risk.

Plan is to continue Lemsip but avoid extra paracetamol: "It's fine to carry on what you're doing at the moment with the lemcip... that contains paracetamol, so don't take any other paracetamol containing products with that."
Doctor advises against cough syrup in daytime: "the cough syrup isn't advisable in the daytime. It's best for your body if you just keep coughing."
Night-time cough syrup allowed if preventing sleep: "if you're kept up all night and you can't sleep at all, then it's okay to have a little bit of cough syrup just to settle that down."
While ongoing management of diabetes and hypertension is implied, there is no explicit instruction phrased as 'continue metformin and lisinopril as prescribed.'
Routine GP follow-up for BP and diabetes is advised: "make sure that you have the regular diabetes and blood pressure checkups that your GPAs ask you for."
Doctor confirms lack of blood sugar checking equipment currently but does not state a plan for future home glucose monitoring.

Doctor educates about red flags and when to recontact: detailed instructions on temperature, worsening cough, purulent phlegm, blood in sputum or nose, shortness of breath, and chest pain with instruction to "speak to you again."
Patient denies chest pain: Doctor: "Any chest pain?" Patient: "No."
Patient denies shortness of breath: Doctor: "Any difficulty breathing, feeling short of breath?" Patient: "No, that's all fine."
No sore throat: Doctor asks about "sore ears, sore throat"; patient does not report sore throat and later mentions only achy muscles as additional symptom, implying negative as per ROS context.
No ear pain: Doctor: "Any other symptoms, like sore. Sore ears, sore throat?" Patient does not endorse sore ears and later lists only achy muscles, indicating denial of ear pain in that ROS check.
No rash: Doctor: "Any rashes that you've noticed?" Patient: "No, nothing like that."
